findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the disposition of the no-leg acquire() raise explicitly (fatal/permanent — no kernel-mediated exclusivity primitive means store writes cannot be safely performed and MUST NOT be retried), distinct from the transient contention path.
evidence: 'with NO exclusive leg available, acquire() raises and never creates .ticket-write.lock.d'
write_lock_is_busy is described as 'an advisory, zero-deadline probe that fails OPEN' — the busy-probe arm HAS a stated disposition, the no-leg raise arm does not
'A userspace substitute that does not die with its holder does NOT satisfy the precondition' implies the no-leg state is unrecoverable, but no disposition word states this
findings.finding: The plan alters two failure arms — write_lock_is_busy 'fails OPEN' and acquire() 'raises' when no exclusive leg is available — but only the fail-open arm carries an explicit disposition. The no-leg acquire() raise has no stated disposition word (fatal/permanent vs retryable): the plan says acquire() 'raises and never creates .ticket-write.lock.d' but not what the caller surfaces, so it is unclear whether a store write on an unsupported platform is a permanent/fatal configuration error (as the logic implies) or something a caller might retry.
findings.location: AC3 / 'What a correct fix requires' item 1
findings.suggested_fix: Add to AC3 that the no-leg raise surfaces a fatal/permanent disposition (e.g. a distinct non-retryable exception type), and confirm the fail-open write_lock_is_busy arm never masks it.

Retrieved (runebook.dev, 'Cross-Platform File Locking in Python: From msvcrt to portalocker'): 'portalocker is a popular choice that handles msvcrt.locking() on Windows and fcntl on POSIX systems automatically.'
Retrieved (github.com/WoLpH/portalocker): 'Portalocker is a library to provide an easy API to file locking.'

ABSENCE: the plan never names portalocker/filelock nor argues why a bespoke selector is preferred (e.g. no-new-dependency policy), so the roll-your-own choice is unjustified vs an established approach.
findings.finding: The plan proposes a hand-rolled stdlib-only Windows exclusive-lock leg (msvcrt.locking / LockFileEx via ctypes) without considering the established cross-platform prior art (the portalocker and filelock libraries) that already abstract exactly the fcntl<->msvcrt seam this story is building by hand.
findings.location: Section 'What a correct fix requires', item 1; ACs 1 and 4
scenarios: A maintainer later discovers filelock/portalocker already solves the fcntl/msvcrt seam with a maintained, tested primitive and questions why lock.py grew a bespoke leg selector.
The bespoke leg has to independently re-derive release-on-death and cross-process semantics that a library has already hardened.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a short 'prior art' note to the story weighing portalocker/filelock (which wrap fcntl on POSIX and msvcrt on Windows) against the stdlib-only selector, and state the deciding constraint (e.g. rebar's dependency policy) that motivates the bespoke path.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Resolve the release-on-process-death capability for the chosen Windows primitive from authoritative docs (and note the contested msvcrt.locking behaviour reported upstream) BEFORE committing, rather than only proving it in the windows-latest CI test — and record which primitive (msvcrt.locking vs LockFileEx) actually satisfies it.
evidence: Plan: 'The whole design rests on two properties of msvcrt.locking: the lock is visible ACROSS PROCESSES, and the kernel releases it when the holding process dies.'
Plan: 'If that test fails, the design is wrong and the story reopens.'

Retrieved (github.com/conan-io/conan issue #6079 title): 'Repo advisory locks fail to release on process termination' — with 'The API used to implement locking on Windows is msvcrt.locking' — a direct contradiction of the release-on-death assumption for msvcrt.locking.
Plan explicitly offers LockFileEx via ctypes as an alternative but does not indicate which primitive actually satisfies release-on-death.
findings.finding: The design's single load-bearing property — that the Windows primitive is released by the kernel when the holding process dies (which keeps _acquire_mkdir's fcntl_held=True honest) — is asserted and deferred to a windows-latest test, but is NOT resolved as a documented capability before committing; retrieved prior art contradicts it for msvcrt advisory locks.
findings.location: Section 'What a correct fix requires' item 5; AC4 ('release-on-process-death ... proved empirically'); item 1 precondition
scenarios: msvcrt.locking is chosen, the CI capability test reveals the byte-range lock is not reliably released on abnormal process exit, and the whole fcntl_held=True staleness proof for the Windows leg is invalid — reopening the story after downstream epic work has been gated on it.
LockFileEx (which is kernel-mediated on the HANDLE and released on process death) would satisfy the property but msvcrt.locking might not, and the plan treats them as interchangeable.
findings.suggested_fix: State explicitly in the story which Windows primitive is chosen and cite its documented release-on-close/process-death semantics; if msvcrt.locking's release-on-death is uncertain (per conan-io/conan#6079), prefer LockFileEx via ctypes on the file HANDLE, which is documented to release on handle close / process termination.
